Agents find it through llms.txt , then look up services and prices, book, cancel or reschedule, and leave the owner a message that they answer from Slack. It is modular: turn on only the connectors you need. Missing one? Open an issue . Quick start Needs Node >= 22.13, git and npm (macOS or Linux; Windows via WSL), plus the system you want agents to book into: a Google Calendar shared with a service account, or a Square Appointments account. The wizard walks you through setup for either ( Google , Square ). curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudroom-ai/gateway/main/install.sh | sh The installer clones into ~/gateway , builds, and runs the setup wizard, which starts by offering to read your website to prefill its questions (optional, and it asks before sending the page text to a model), then asks what you want agents to do. It writes config.json and .env , checks access, and prints the next steps: start the server with npm start and check it locally. Re-run it to update; npm run init re-opens the wizard, which asks whether to keep, review or start over. Details, manual install and the read-it-first variant: docs/install.md . The API (services, slots, quotes, booking, cancel, reschedule, owner messages) is described in docs/agents.md and served at /openapi.json . Demo To repeat this recording with your own agent, give the local server a public HTTPS address (cloud agents can't reach localhost ) and hand the agent the link. Needs cloudflared ( brew install cloudflared ). # Terminal 1: open a tunnel. It prints https://<tunnel-host>.trycloudflare.com cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000 # Terminal 2: start Gateway and let it answer on that hostname cd ~ /gateway && ALLOWED_HOSTS= < tunnel-host > .trycloudflare.com,localhost,127.0.0.1 npm start Then ask your agent (Muse, Grok or similar), filling in one of your services: Book me a <service> on Friday at 10am using https://<tunnel-host>.trycloudflare.com My name is <name> and my phone number is <phone>. The agent reads the instructions served there (the same page as /llms.txt ), checks slots, gets a quote and books, and the event shows up in your calendar. The tunnel hostname changes on every run, and ChatGPT refuses trycloudflare.com links, so use a real domain for anything longer-lived ( docs/deploy.md §3 ). Connectors Connectors come in three modules. A Store is a booking platform that owns its slots and prices. A Calendar is a plain calendar that Gateway builds slots and prices on. Communication is how the owner hears from Gateway, and it works beside either of the others. System Module Doc Google Calendar (service account) Calendar: Gateway builds slots and prices from your rules docs/connectors/google.md Square Appointments Store: Square's catalog, prices and policies; buyer-level access, no payments docs/connectors/square.md GlossGenius (experimental) Store, shadow mode: services, prices and open times read from the public booking page; bookings go to a shared Google Calendar plus a text to the merchant, who adds them to GlossGenius docs/connectors/glossgenius.md Twilio SMS (optional) Communication, notices only: texts the merchant about every agent booking, cancel and reschedule docs/connectors/twilio.md Slack (optional) Communication, two-way: agent messages land in a Slack channel and the owner answers by typing in the thread; booking notices too. Socket Mode, no inbound URL docs/connectors/slack.md Adding a connector: docs/connectors/README.md . Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md . Docs docs/install.md : installer, wizard, manual install, updating docs/configuration.md : config.json and every env var docs/deploy.md : Docker, HTTPS tunnel, hosting, operations docs/agents.md : llms.txt , openapi.json , HTTP smoke test, booking semantics docs/errors.md , docs/architecture.md , docs/README.md (index) License Apache-2.0. post.title: A booking gateway for AI agents
post.promise: See how a small service could let agents check services, prices and booking slots.
post.whatItIs: Gateway is an open-source server that exposes a business's services, prices and booking actions to AI agents over HTTP. A beginner's experiment could help one local service business set up and test this flow; that service offer is hypothetical. The documented setup needs Node, npm, a calendar or Square account, and configuration.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: an appointment-based business might pay for setup help if it wants agents to handle booking requests. The source documents no paying customers or revenue.
loop: The owner lists services and prices in the chosen booking system.
Gateway exposes the information and available slots to an agent.
The agent checks a requested slot and gets a quote.
The agent submits a booking, cancellation or rescheduling request.
The owner reviews the calendar and handles messages or exceptions.
post.evidence: The project README describes Google Calendar and Square connectors, an API for services, slots, quotes and bookings, and a demo in which an agent checks a slot, gets a quote and books into a calendar. It documents prerequisites and setup. This shows a working-product path, not customer adoption.
post.uncertainty: The demo requires configuration and a public HTTPS address for a cloud agent; its temporary tunnel changes each run. Human owners still need to check calendar accuracy, permissions, messages and exceptions. The source gives no evidence of demand or paid users.
first24Hours: Read the README's quick-start prerequisites and write down which are available; completion is a checklist showing Node, npm and a test calendar or Square account status.
Draw a sample service, price and booking flow without using real customer data; completion is a diagram with the owner review point marked.
Ask one appointment business whether this hypothetical workflow is useful, without promising results; completion is a dated note of their answer or no response.

ease.reason: The README gives a quick start, but setup needs Node 22.13+, npm, Git and a connected booking system.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: appointment businesses could value agent booking, but the page reports no paying customers or validated demand.

feasibility.reason: A narrow demo is documented, though a beginner must configure a calendar or Square and expose a reachable server.

autonomy.reason: The documented flow checks slots and can book, while owner messages and setup, permissions and exceptions need human handling.

evidence.reason: The README describes connectors, setup and a repeatable booking demonstration, but gives no evidence of real customer use.

post.title: A server for AI appointment requests
post.promise: Gateway lets agents check services, prices and slots before requesting a booking.
post.whatItIs: Gateway is an open-source server for businesses to publish services and prices to AI agents over HTTP. Its README describes connecting a Google Calendar or Square Appointments, then allowing agents to check availability, get a quote, book, cancel or reschedule. A beginner experiment could test a narrowly scoped setup for one service, if they have access to the required calendar or Square account.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: an appointment-based business that wants to accept AI-agent bookings might pay for setup or support. The source does not establish customers or revenue.
loop: Choose one service and its price with the business owner.
Set up Gateway and connect an available Google Calendar or Square account.
Check the published service and available slots locally.
Let an agent request a quote and booking through the server.
Have the owner review bookings, cancellations and messages, then correct setup issues.
post.evidence: The GitHub README describes an open-source server with services, prices, booking and owner messages over HTTP, and a demo in which an agent checks slots, gets a quote and books into a calendar. It lists Node 22.13 or newer and a Google Calendar service account or Square account as setup requirements.
post.uncertainty: The page documents a demo and setup path, not customer demand or production reliability. The demo requires a reachable HTTPS address for a cloud agent. A human must confirm service details, access, and whether each booking or change is appropriate; the source does not establish unattended operation safety.
first24Hours: Read the README setup requirements and choose a test calendar or Square account you are authorized to use.
Write down one service, its price and the booking rules with its owner.
Map a local test of slot lookup and a booking request, with owner review before any real appointment is accepted.

ease.reason: A one-service trial is conceivable, but the README requires Node, npm, Git and calendar or Square setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: appointment businesses might pay for booking setup, but the source reports no customers or revenue.

feasibility.reason: The documented quick start and demo give a bounded trial, with account setup and HTTPS access as obstacles.

autonomy.reason: The server supports repeatable slot checks and booking actions, while owners provide service rules and handle messages and review.

evidence.reason: The README provides setup steps and a repeatable demo, but no independent real-use evidence.

post.title: A remote browser for AI agents
post.promise: Browser Use offers hosted browsers that an agent can use to complete web tasks.
post.whatItIs: Browser Use describes two products: Browser Use Agents, a web agent, and Browser Infrastructure, a remote browser for other agents. A beginner can study the documented product and try a small, low-stakes browser task; a student-built service that automates a narrow task would be a separate hypothesis, not an established feature here.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a team running agents on web tasks might pay for browser infrastructure or agent access. The page lists pricing, but does not establish paying customer counts.
loop: Choose a permitted, low-stakes task on a site you are allowed to use.
Connect an agent to Browser Use using its documented starting path.
Have the agent attempt the selected browser task.
Check the page state and any submitted information yourself.
Record where the agent failed and decide whether to retry manually.
post.evidence: The first-party page describes Browser Use Agents and Browser Infrastructure and gives pricing for browser time and agent usage. It reports results from its own 106-task and 71-site benchmarks; these are company-reported tests, not independent proof of customer outcomes.
post.uncertainty: The provided page does not give beginner implementation instructions or detailed evidence for a student-built service. Benchmark methods and real-world outcomes are not independently established in this source. Keep a person responsible for account access, sensitive data, and any consequential form submission or purchase.
first24Hours: Read the product and pricing sections and pick one low-stakes web task.
Try the available free starting option only on a site and account you may use.
Check the result manually and list which actions would need human approval in a repeatable trial.

ease.reason: The page offers a free start but supplies little implementation detail for a beginner experiment.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: teams operating web agents might pay; listed prices do not show buyer demand or revenue.

feasibility.reason: A product trial is bounded, but the supplied page does not explain how to build a student version in two weeks.

autonomy.reason: The product is presented as agents completing browser tasks, but this source gives no operational loop or human-review details.

evidence.reason: The first-party page describes products and benchmarks, without independent verification or specific customer-use evidence.

A student could hypothetically test one low-risk public-page research workflow for a small organization, with a person checking every result; this service is not established by the source.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small organization that repeats public web research might pay for a reviewed summary. The page provides product pricing, not evidence that such customers buy this proposed service.
loop: The user chooses a permitted public page and a narrow question.
An agent uses a browser to gather the requested page information.
The agent returns a draft summary with links to the pages it used.
A person checks the pages and corrects errors before sharing anything.
The person records failures and stops tasks involving access barriers or sensitive actions.
post.evidence: The product page describes Browser Use Agents and remote browser infrastructure, says the service supports examples including data extraction and research, and lists browser infrastructure at $0.02 per hour plus internet traffic. Its benchmark figures are company-reported claims on the page, not independent validation here.
post.uncertainty: The page does not establish how reliably a beginner's chosen workflow will perform or whether an organization would pay for it. Browser tasks can fail or return wrong information, so a human must check source pages; do not use this experiment for logins, sensitive data or consequential submissions.

Review the product's free-start and pricing information and estimate the test inputs; completion is a note of listed charges and unknown traffic cost.
Manually answer the question from the page and save the supporting lines; completion is a checked answer with its source URL.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: organizations may value reviewed web research, but the page shows product pricing rather than demand for this service.

feasibility.reason: A single public-page task is a plausible small experiment, though setup, usage costs and task reliability are not established here.

autonomy.reason: The product is presented for browser agents and research, but a human must verify outputs and handle failures in this proposed loop.

evidence.reason: The page describes live agent and infrastructure products, use examples and pricing; its benchmark claims are first-party and not independently confirmed here.

Keep what matters. A local-first, open-source meeting assistant for Apple Silicon Macs. Get Pluto · Privacy · Setup guide · Releases Pluto records meetings without a bot, transcribes on your Mac, and connects conversations into a working memory of people, projects, and follow-ups. Your meetings, commitments, and recent wins in one place. Screenshots use fictional demo data. Get started You’ll need an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) with macOS 14.2 or later . 1. Install Pluto Open Terminal, paste this command, and press Return: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metagrover/pluto/master/scripts/install-macos.sh | bash Pluto installs and opens. Follow setup to choose your storage options, download speech models, and allow microphone and system audio access. 2. Set up local AI Download Ollama for Mac , open it, and complete its command-line setup. Then run these commands in Terminal to download the models for meeting notes and chat: ollama pull gemma4:12b ollama pull phi4-mini:3.8b Keep Ollama running. In Pluto’s Settings → Intelligence , use Ollama with Gemma 4 12B for analysis and Phi-4 Mini for fast chat—the defaults for new setups. These are separate from the speech models downloaded during setup. Prefer a cloud provider? Choose one in Settings → Intelligence and add your API key instead of setting up Ollama. 3. Try your first meeting Click New meeting , record a short conversation, and stop when you’re done. Once processing finishes, review the notes and next steps, then ask a question about the conversation. Let participants know when you record. Full setup guide and troubleshooting → · Download a DMG instead → From conversation to context Start with a meeting. Return to the decisions, connect them to earlier conversations, and carry that context into whatever comes next. Keep the decisions, not just the recording Review notes and next steps. Confirm familiar speakers with Voice ID, and follow People and Projects across conversations. Ask. Then check the source. Ask about your meeting history and follow the references back to the conversation. Pick up the thread in ChatGPT The optional Pluto plugin brings meeting notes into ChatGPT on the same Mac. Install Pluto and choose local AI setup, following its guide.
Record a short meeting with participant permission.
Review the generated notes and next steps against the conversation.
Ask a question about the meeting and follow its references back to the source.
post.evidence: The GitHub README provides Mac setup steps, names an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 14.2 or later, and describes recording, transcription, notes, next steps and source references. It explicitly tells users to let participants know when recording.

Local processing is described, but the provided text does not establish every privacy property.

post.title: Turn meeting recordings into reviewed notes
post.promise: Try Pluto's local meeting workflow, then check notes against the conversation.
post.whatItIs: Pluto is an open-source meeting assistant for Apple Silicon Macs. Its README says it records meetings without a bot, transcribes on the Mac, and creates notes and next steps. A student could hypothetically offer help organizing reviewed notes for a small team, using only meetings whose participants agreed to recording.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small team that wants help keeping track of meeting decisions might pay for setup or note organization. The page does not establish paying customers for that service.
loop: Tell participants about the recording and get their agreement before starting.
Record a short meeting in Pluto on a supported Mac.
Let Pluto process the recording into notes and next steps.
Review the notes against the conversation and correct errors.
Share only the approved notes with the intended participants.
post.evidence: The README describes Pluto's local recording and transcription flow, lists Apple Silicon and macOS requirements, and instructs users to review notes and next steps after processing. It also says screenshots use fictional demo data. This is first-party product documentation, not evidence of customer outcomes.
post.uncertainty: A suitable Mac, model downloads and microphone and system-audio permissions are required. Transcription or generated notes may be wrong; people must consent to recording and check the notes before sharing. The source does not demonstrate paid demand for a note service.
first24Hours: Check the README's Mac and macOS requirements against your device; completion is a written yes or no for each requirement.
Draft a short consent message explaining the recording and ask participants before any test; completion is their recorded agreement or a decision not to record.
If everyone agrees and setup is available, record a short test meeting and compare each proposed next step with the audio; completion is a corrected note or a log that setup prevented the test.

ease.reason: The README gives an install and first-meeting path, but requires Apple Silicon, macOS 14.2 or later and model setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: teams may value organized meeting notes, but the supplied page gives no evidence of buyers for a student note service.

feasibility.reason: A single short meeting is a bounded trial with documented setup steps, contingent on supported hardware and participant consent.

autonomy.reason: Pluto can record, transcribe and draft notes locally, while consent, error correction and sharing decisions stay with people.

evidence.reason: The first-party README documents a working product and first-meeting workflow, but its sample screenshots use fictional data and real-use outcomes are not shown.
